events.title: The September 11 attacks
events.description: Terrorist attacks kill thousands of people in the United States. Communities mourn and help those affected.

events.title: Apple introduces the iPod
events.description: A pocket-sized digital music player becomes a new product for the computer maker.

events.title: Microsoft and the US government propose a settlement
events.description: The agreement would restrict some business practices. Court review and other legal steps remain.

events.title: Euro cash enters everyday use
events.description: Twelve countries introduce euro notes and coins.

events.title: Columbia is lost
events.description: The space shuttle breaks apart during its return to Earth, killing its seven crew members.

what_happened_next.text:
Apple ended this window about 41% above its starting value, while Cisco ended about 70% lower and Microsoft about 30% lower. Bonds gained as the U.S. share basket fell. Being part of the technology industry did not give these companies the same result, and Apple’s final gain hid a rough path.

Company news gives useful context. Apple said more than two million iPods had sold by January 2004, showing demand for a product beyond computers. Cisco reported a $2.2 billion charge for unsold equipment and a $2.69 billion loss in 2001. Microsoft announced a $3 one-time dividend in 2004, scheduled for payment that December. These stories mattered to the businesses and their shareholders, but none alone explains the five-year ending value.

The period included the September 11 attacks, the arrival of euro cash and the Columbia shuttle disaster. People faced changes and losses far beyond their investment accounts. Finishing above the starting point does not mean an investment never fell below it; anyone forced to sell during a bad month would have had a different experience. A lawsuit or promising device could not tell someone exactly when prices would turn.

reflection.what_people_were_focused_on: Korean diplomacy, digital music and Microsoft’s court case were prominent. People were also discovering new museums and returning to everyday hobbies.
reflection.what_actually_mattered: Different businesses and asset types mattered more than one broad label such as technology. A portfolio concentrated in a few famous names faced large company risks.
reflection.what_faded_away: The first reaction to a court order did not explain the complete investment result. Neither did the latest online trading tool.
reflection.what_nobody_knew: The precise winners and losses were unknown. An investor could not know in advance how a promising product, a lawsuit or a major world event would affect the final value.

hot:2000-06:microsoft.text: In July 2004, Microsoft announced a one-time $3-per-share dividend for December, along with regular dividends and a share-buyback plan. The payout returned company cash directly to shareholders and added a cash payment to the value of owning Microsoft shares.

hot:2000-06:cisco.text: On May 8, 2001, Cisco reported quarterly sales of $4.73 billion, down 4% from a year earlier. It recorded a $2.2 billion charge for excess inventory and a $2.69 billion net loss as orders for networking equipment slowed sharply.

hot:2000-06:apple.text: Apple said on January 6, 2004, that more than two million iPods had sold since launch. The music player expanded Apple beyond Mac computers and made its iTunes software more useful to customers carrying a portable library of songs.
